stem: What is Artificial Intelligence, at the broadest definition?

options.text: Any system designed to perform tasks that would normally require human intelligence
Only robots with human-like bodies
options.misconception: Takes the popular image of AI for the definition, excluding the software that makes up almost all of it.

options.text: A synonym for very large amounts of data
options.misconception: Confuses an ingredient with the field itself.

options.text: Software that never makes mistakes
options.misconception: Treats reliability as the defining property, when AI systems are often probabilistic and wrong.

hints: Ask whether the definition should cover a chess program from 1997 as well as a chatbot.
The broad definition is about the kind of task, not the kind of hardware.
explanation_after: The broad definition covers any system doing work that would otherwise need human intelligence — planning, recognising, translating. It is deliberately wide, which is why 'AI' has meant different things in different decades.

stem: What is an 'AI winter'?

options.text: A cooling system for the data centres that train large models
options.misconception: Reads the term literally as hardware infrastructure.

options.text: The season when the major AI research conferences take place
options.misconception: Reads it as calendar jargon rather than as a description of the field's funding cycles.

options.text: The phase of training where a model's loss stops improving
options.misconception: Borrows a plausible training-dynamics meaning for what is a historical term.

options.text: A period of reduced funding and interest after earlier hype failed to deliver

hints: The term describes what happened to the field, not to a machine.
Ask what follows a period of promises that were not met.
explanation_after: An AI winter is a funding and interest collapse following unmet expectations; there were two major ones. The pattern is worth knowing because the hype-and-correction cycle has recurred.

stem: How do AI, Machine Learning and Deep Learning relate to each other?

options.text: They are three unrelated fields
options.misconception: Misses that each is contained in the one before.

options.text: Deep Learning is the broadest, containing AI and ML
options.misconception: Has the nesting inverted, usually from meeting deep learning first.

options.text: Nested: Deep Learning sits inside Machine Learning, which sits inside AI
They are the same thing under three names
options.misconception: Collapses a hierarchy; a rule-based expert system is AI but not ML.

hints: Ask whether every AI system learns from data, and whether every learning system uses neural networks.
Try to think of something in the outer category that is not in the inner one.
explanation_after: AI is the widest; ML is the part that learns from data; deep learning is the part of ML using many-layered networks. A hand-written rules engine is AI but not ML, which is what the nesting captures.

stem: In reinforcement learning, what does the model learn from?

options.text: A labelled answer for every input
options.misconception: Describes supervised learning, where the correct output is given directly.

options.text: Clusters discovered in unlabelled data
options.misconception: Describes unsupervised learning, which has no feedback signal at all.

options.text: A copy of an expert's exact actions
options.misconception: Describes imitation learning; reinforcement learning can discover behaviour nobody demonstrated.

options.text: Rewards or penalties received after taking actions

hints: Think about training a dog rather than marking an exam.
Ask what tells the system it did well, when nobody says what the right move was.
explanation_after: Reinforcement learning receives a reward signal after acting, rather than being told the correct action. That is why it can find strategies no human demonstrated — and why shaping the reward is so delicate.

stem: What is a test set?

options.text: Data held back from training, used once to estimate performance on unseen data
The portion of data the model trains on most carefully
options.misconception: Inverts the purpose; the test set is precisely what the model never trains on.

options.text: Data used to tune settings like the learning rate
options.misconception: Describes the validation set, which is a third split with a different job.

options.text: A set of unit tests for the training code
options.misconception: Reads 'test' in the software-engineering sense rather than the statistical one.

hints: Ask what question the set exists to answer, and why the model must not have seen it.
There are usually three splits; this is the one touched last.
explanation_after: The test set stands in for data the model will meet in the wild, so it must stay unseen. Tuning against it repeatedly turns it into a validation set and quietly inflates the reported score.

stem: In machine learning, what is a 'feature'?

options.text: A capability of the software product
options.misconception: Reads the word in its product-management sense rather than its modelling sense.

options.text: An individual measurable input the model uses to make its prediction
The output the model predicts
options.misconception: Confuses feature with label or target — the thing being predicted, not predicted from.

options.text: A layer inside a neural network
options.misconception: Confuses the data going in with the architecture processing it.

hints: In a spreadsheet of training data, ask what the columns are.
One column is special because it is the answer; the rest are this.
explanation_after: A feature is one input column — square footage, word count, hour of day. The target is what you predict; everything else you predict from is a feature.

stem: Why is training a machine learning model fundamentally different from writing if/else rules?

options.text: Training is the same thing with different syntax
options.misconception: Misses that nobody writes the decision boundary in the learned case.

options.text: Hand-written rules are always more accurate than trained models
options.misconception: Makes an accuracy claim where the difference is about who determines the rules.

options.text: Training adjusts internal numeric parameters from data until predictions improve, instead of a human writing out every rule
Training only works on image data
options.misconception: Invents a domain restriction unrelated to the distinction.

hints: Ask who decides the exact threshold at which a decision flips, in each case.
Consider a task where you could not write the rules down even if you wanted to — recognising a face, say.
explanation_after: With rules, a human states every condition. With training, the conditions are numeric parameters fitted from examples. That is why ML suits tasks we can demonstrate but cannot articulate — and why the resulting rules are hard to read back.

stem: Why does supervised learning need labelled data when unsupervised learning does not?

options.text: Unsupervised learning is simply an easier version of supervised learning
options.misconception: Treats them as the same task at different difficulty, rather than different tasks.

options.text: There is no real difference between the two approaches
options.misconception: Denies a distinction that determines what data you must collect.

options.text: Labels are only needed for images, not text
options.misconception: Invents a modality rule; labels follow from the task, not the data type.

options.text: Supervised learning compares its guess against a known answer, which must therefore exist; unsupervised learning looks for structure with no answer to check against

hints: Ask what the training process actually computes in order to improve.
If there is no correct answer recorded, what could an error be measured against?
explanation_after: Supervised training needs an error, and an error needs a truth to compare with. Unsupervised methods look for structure — clusters, components — where no single answer is defined, which is why they are judged so differently.

stem: Why does 'garbage in, garbage out' apply especially strongly to machine learning?

options.text: Because computers physically slow down when given bad data
options.misconception: Reads a correctness problem as a performance one.

options.text: It does not apply — models correct for bad data automatically
options.misconception: Attributes a judgment to the model that nothing in training provides.

options.text: It only applies to unsupervised learning
options.misconception: Restricts the principle arbitrarily; mislabelled supervised data is the clearest case of all.

options.text: Because the model learns whatever pattern is actually in the data, including bias and mislabelling, with no way to know better

hints: Ask what the model would have to possess in order to notice the data was wrong.
Consider what a model learns from a thousand examples labelled by a careless annotator.
explanation_after: A model has no outside knowledge to check its data against; it fits whatever is there, faithfully. Flawed data produces a confidently wrong model, and the flaw is usually invisible in the metrics.

stem: Why does deep learning usually need far more data than classical machine learning?

options.text: Because it has many more parameters to fit, and it learns the features itself rather than being given them
Because neural networks read each example more slowly
options.misconception: Frames a statistical requirement as a speed issue.

options.text: Because deep learning cannot use numeric data
options.misconception: Invents a data-type restriction that does not exist.

options.text: Because its data has to be labelled twice for accuracy
options.misconception: Invents a labelling requirement; the labels are the same either way.

hints: Count roughly how many numbers each kind of model has to determine from the data.
Ask who supplies the features in each case — the engineer, or the model?
explanation_after: Classical models fit a handful of parameters over features a person designed. A deep network fits millions and discovers the features too, so it needs far more examples to pin them down — which is why small datasets often favour the classical approach.

stem: How does underfitting differ from overfitting?

options.text: Underfitting means the model is too slow; overfitting means it is too fast
options.misconception: Reads both terms as being about speed rather than about fit.

options.text: Underfitting performs poorly on training and new data alike; overfitting does well on training data and poorly on new data
Underfitting only happens with too much data; overfitting with too little
options.misconception: Half-right about overfitting, but underfitting comes from too simple a model, not from abundance.

options.text: They are two names for the same failure
options.misconception: Collapses two opposite problems that call for opposite fixes.

hints: Compare the training score and the unseen score in each case.
One model has not learned enough; the other has learned too much of the wrong thing.
explanation_after: Underfitting is bad everywhere: the model is too simple to capture the pattern. Overfitting is good on seen data and bad on unseen. The fixes are opposite — more capacity versus more regularisation — so naming it right matters.

stem: Why is training typically far more expensive than inference?

options.text: Because inference skips most of the model's layers
options.misconception: Inference runs the whole network; what it skips is the backward pass.

options.text: Because training requires an internet connection
options.misconception: Confuses a deployment detail with where the computational cost lies.

options.text: Because training passes over the data many times and computes updates for every parameter each time, while inference is a single forward pass
Because training uses more precise arithmetic
options.misconception: Precision does differ in practice, but it is a minor factor beside the number of passes.

hints: Count the passes: how many times does each process see an example?
Ask what extra work has to happen after a prediction during training, that never happens in production.
explanation_after: Inference is one forward pass. Training repeats that pass over millions of examples for many epochs and adds a backward pass computing gradients for every parameter — hence weeks on a cluster to train, milliseconds to serve.

stem: A chatbot generating a live reply to a user's message right now is an example of:

options.text: Training
options.misconception: Assumes the model learns from each conversation as it happens, which a deployed model generally does not.

options.text: Inference
Labelling
options.misconception: Confuses producing an output with annotating data for later training.

options.text: Overfitting
options.misconception: Names a training failure mode rather than an activity.

hints: Ask whether the model's parameters change while it answers.
One of these is what happens before deployment; the other is what happens after.
explanation_after: Using a trained model to produce an output is inference. The weights are fixed; nothing is learned from this conversation unless that data is later collected for a training run.

stem: A model correctly classifies 85 of 100 test examples. What is its accuracy?

options.misconception: Misplaces the decimal when converting a proportion to a percentage.
Reports the error rate rather than the accuracy.

options.text: It cannot be determined from this information
options.misconception: Accuracy needs only correct over total, both of which are given.

hints: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions.
Check whether your answer describes what went right or what went wrong.
explanation_after: 85/100 = 85%. Worth remembering that accuracy alone says nothing about which 15 were wrong — on an imbalanced problem, that omission matters enormously.

stem: A model scores 99% on its training data but 55% on new data. This pattern is called:

options.text: Underfitting
options.misconception: Underfitting would score poorly on the training data too.

options.text: Perfect generalisation
options.misconception: Generalisation is exactly what the 55% shows is absent.

options.text: Inference
options.misconception: Names an activity rather than a diagnosis.

options.text: Overfitting

hints: The gap between the two scores is the diagnostic signal.
Ask whether the model learned the pattern or the examples.
explanation_after: A large gap between training and unseen performance is the definition of overfitting: the model memorised its examples rather than learning what generalises.

stem: A shop has purchase histories for 50,000 customers and no categories defined. They want to discover natural customer groupings. Which kind of learning fits?

options.text: Supervised classification
options.misconception: Requires categories to predict, and the stem says none are defined.

options.text: Unsupervised clustering
Supervised regression
options.misconception: Predicts a number from labelled examples; there is no target here either.

options.text: Reinforcement learning
options.misconception: Needs actions and a reward signal; nothing here is acting or being rewarded.

hints: Ask whether there is a correct answer recorded anywhere in the data.
The goal is to discover groups, not to predict a known one.
explanation_after: No labels and a goal of finding structure points squarely at clustering. If the shop later defines segments by hand and wants to assign new customers to them, that becomes a supervised problem.

stem: You have 10,000 labelled examples and plan an 80/10/10 split. How many examples does the model actually learn from?

options.text: 10,000 — all data is used for learning eventually
options.misconception: Misses that the held-out portions must never be learned from, or they stop measuring anything.

options.text: 9,000 — training plus validation
options.misconception: Counts validation as learning; it steers choices but no weights are fitted on it.

options.text: 1,000 — only the test set gives real evidence
options.misconception: Confuses the set used for measuring with the set used for fitting.

hints: Name what each of the three portions is for before counting any of them.
Only one of the three updates the model's parameters.
explanation_after: 80% trains, 10% validates tuning choices, 10% is the final untouched test. Validation influences decisions without fitting weights, which is why it is not training data and still not a fair final score.

stem: A thermostat switches the heating on below 18°C and off above 21°C. Is it AI, machine learning, both, or neither?

options.text: Both, because it makes decisions automatically
options.misconception: Treats any automatic decision as learned; nothing here was fitted from data.

options.text: Machine learning, because it responds to its environment
options.misconception: Responding to input is not learning; the thresholds were set by a person.

options.text: Neither in the modern sense: it follows fixed rules a person wrote, and learns nothing
AI but not ML, because any automated control counts as AI
options.misconception: Stretches the broad definition until it covers all automation, which empties it of content.

hints: Ask whether anything about the device changes with experience.
Ask who chose the numbers 18 and 21.
explanation_after: The thresholds were written by a person and never change, so there is no learning. A thermostat that observed your habits and adjusted its own schedule would be machine learning — the dividing line is whether data changes the behaviour.

stem: A house-price model does poorly with only 'square footage'. Adding 'square footage per bedroom' improves it markedly. Why would a derived feature help where the raw one did not?

options.text: It does not really help; this is coincidence
options.misconception: Dismisses a measured improvement rather than explaining it.

options.text: Square footage should never be used as a feature
options.misconception: Rejects a useful raw feature instead of explaining what the ratio adds to it.

options.text: Adding any new feature always improves a model
options.misconception: Irrelevant features add noise and can make a model worse, especially on small data.

options.text: It expresses a relationship — space relative to room count — that neither raw number states on its own

hints: Compare two houses with the same floor area but two and six bedrooms, and ask what differs.
Ask what a linear model can and cannot construct from the raw columns by itself.
explanation_after: A ratio encodes a relationship a linear model cannot form from the raw columns alone. Feature engineering is largely about making an existing relationship explicit enough for the model to use.

stem: A model tested well but its accuracy quietly degrades over months in production, although the model was never changed. What does that indicate?

options.text: The original test results must have been fabricated
options.misconception: Reaches for misconduct when an ordinary and well-documented mechanism explains it.

options.text: Models always get worse over time regardless of data
options.misconception: Treats decay as inevitable rather than as a consequence of the world changing.

options.text: Data or concept drift: the live data has moved away from the distribution the model was trained on
The server needs more memory
options.misconception: Resource limits would affect latency or availability, not gradual accuracy decline.

hints: The model is fixed, so ask what else could have changed.
Consider what a model trained on last year's customers faces this year.
explanation_after: Frozen weights meeting a shifting world is drift. It is why production models need monitoring and periodic retraining — the launch score is a snapshot, not a guarantee.

stem: Training loss falls steadily every epoch, while validation loss falls at first and then climbs. What does the shape reveal about when overfitting began?

options.text: It began at the first epoch
options.misconception: Ignores the early phase where both losses improved together, which is genuine learning.

options.text: At the point validation loss stopped falling and began to rise, even as training loss kept falling
This pattern means the model never overfits
options.misconception: Describes the textbook overfitting signature as its opposite.

options.text: The training curve is irrelevant to detecting overfitting
options.misconception: The divergence between the two curves is the signal; one curve alone cannot show it.

hints: Overfitting is about a gap, so look for where the two curves start to part.
Ask which epoch's weights you would actually want to keep.
explanation_after: The divergence point is where the model stops learning the pattern and starts memorising examples. Early stopping is exactly the practice of keeping the weights from that point.

stem: A fraud detector reports 99.2% accuracy. Fraud is 0.8% of transactions, and the confusion matrix shows zero transactions predicted as fraud. What has the model learned?

options.text: A genuinely strong rule for separating fraud from normal transactions
options.misconception: Reads the headline number without checking that one class is never predicted at all.

options.text: Nothing useful: it predicts 'not fraud' every time, which is right 99.2% of the time and catches no fraud
That the fraud examples were mislabelled
options.misconception: Possible in general, but the matrix here is explained entirely by the class imbalance.

options.text: That accuracy was computed incorrectly
options.misconception: The accuracy is arithmetically correct — that is precisely what makes it misleading.

hints: Work out what accuracy a model would get by always answering the majority class.
The matrix says one column is empty. Ask what prediction rule produces that.
explanation_after: Always answering the majority class scores 99.2% here and catches nothing. On imbalanced problems accuracy is close to useless, which is why precision, recall and the matrix itself are reported instead.

stem: A model separating photos of wolves from huskies does well in testing but fails in the field. Inspection shows it keys on snow in the background. How did that happen?

options.text: The model was too small to learn about animals
options.misconception: Capacity was sufficient to fit the data; the issue is which pattern was easiest, not whether one could be learned.

options.text: Snow is genuinely part of what makes an animal a wolf
options.misconception: Accepts the shortcut as the concept, which is exactly the error the field failure exposes.

options.text: The training wolf photos mostly had snow, so background predicted the label as well as the animal and was easier to learn
The labels were randomly assigned
options.misconception: Random labels would prevent learning anything that tested well in the first place.

hints: The model minimises error on the data it is given. Ask what the cheapest way to do that was.
Ask what the training photos had in common besides the animal.
explanation_after: Training rewards whatever predicts the label, and a correlated background can be easier to detect than anatomy. Shortcut learning is why held-out data drawn from the same biased collection does not catch the problem.

stem: Neural networks were described in the 1950s but only became dominant after about 2012. Which combination best explains the delay?

options.text: The mathematics of backpropagation was not discovered until 2012
options.misconception: Backpropagation was in use in the 1980s; theory was not the missing piece.

options.text: Earlier researchers were not interested in the approach
options.misconception: Attributes to disinterest what was a practical ceiling on data and compute.

options.text: Large labelled datasets and parallel GPU compute arrived together, making deep networks trainable at last
Programming languages before 2012 could not express a neural network
options.misconception: Invents a tooling barrier; networks were implemented decades earlier.

hints: Ask what a deep network needs in quantity, beyond a correct algorithm.
Think about what became available around then — both in data and in hardware.
explanation_after: The ideas largely existed; what arrived was ImageNet-scale labelled data and GPUs capable of the arithmetic. It is a useful case of a method waiting for its inputs rather than for its theory.

stem: For a rare-disease screening model where missing a real case is far costlier than a false alarm, is accuracy or recall the better primary metric, and why?

options.text: Accuracy, because it is simplest to explain to stakeholders
options.misconception: Optimises for communication over the thing the system exists to do.

options.text: Accuracy, because rare-disease datasets are naturally balanced
options.misconception: Rare means imbalanced by definition, which is what breaks accuracy here.

options.text: Neither matters — any metric works equally well
options.misconception: Denies that the choice of metric determines which errors the model is tuned to avoid.

options.text: Recall, because accuracy can look high on rare-disease data while missing most real cases, whereas recall measures how many were caught

hints: Work out what accuracy a model would get by declaring everyone healthy.
Match the metric to the error the stem says is expensive.
explanation_after: Declaring everyone healthy scores extremely well on accuracy and catches nothing. Recall counts the real cases found, which is the quantity the cost structure actually cares about — at the price of more false alarms.

stem: A company wants an AI system to make final hiring decisions with no human review. Judged against what is known about model limitations, is that sound?

options.text: Yes — AI systems are more objective than humans
options.misconception: Mistakes the absence of a human for the absence of bias; the bias arrives through the training data.

options.text: Yes — a deployed model does not make mistakes
options.misconception: Attributes a reliability no model has.

options.text: No: high-stakes decisions about people are exactly where learned bias plus no accountable decision-maker causes real harm
It does not matter, since decisions can be reversed later
options.misconception: Assumes harm is undone by reversal, and that rejected candidates would ever know to appeal.

hints: Ask where the model's idea of a good hire came from, and whose past decisions that reflects.
Ask who a rejected candidate would appeal to, and what that person could examine.
explanation_after: A model trained on past hiring learns past preferences, including discriminatory ones, and removing the human removes the accountable party. The stakes are what make review essential — the same model as a shortlisting aid is a different proposition.

stem: A feature must work instantly and with no internet connection. Should inference run on a cloud GPU or on the user's phone, and why?

options.text: Cloud GPU, because cloud servers are always faster
options.misconception: Compares raw hardware while ignoring the network hop and the offline requirement.

options.text: It makes no difference to offline operation
options.misconception: Denies the constraint the question is built on.

options.text: Cloud GPU, because training and inference must happen in the same place
options.misconception: Invents a coupling; models are routinely trained centrally and run on devices.

options.text: On-device, because the offline requirement rules out a server, and it removes the network round trip too

hints: One of the two requirements eliminates an option outright before any speed comparison.
Ask what a faster server is worth when there is no connection to reach it.
explanation_after: 'No internet' is a hard constraint, not a preference, so the server is out regardless of its speed. The cost is a smaller model on weaker hardware — which is why on-device models are quantised and distilled.

stem: A loan-default model jumps from 71% to 99% accuracy after adding the feature 'debt sent to collections'. A colleague wants to ship it. Assess that.

options.text: Ship it — a 28-point gain is strong evidence the feature is valuable
options.misconception: Treats a suspiciously large jump as a success rather than as a signal to look harder.

options.text: Do not ship: collections happen after a default, so the feature leaks the answer and will not exist at prediction time
Ship it, but retrain monthly to keep the gain
options.misconception: Accepts the leak and schedules it to recur; retraining cannot fix a feature unavailable at decision time.

options.text: Do not ship — 99% accuracy is impossible, so the data must be corrupted
options.misconception: Right conclusion from a wrong premise; the number is real, it just measures the wrong thing.

hints: Ask when each feature's value becomes known, relative to the moment the prediction is needed.
A sudden large jump is usually worth distrusting. Ask what the new column is really recording.
explanation_after: Collections follow a default, so the feature encodes the outcome. The model scores brilliantly offline and is useless at decision time, when the column is empty. Target leakage looks exactly like success, which is what makes it dangerous.

stem: A team proposes retraining their production model nightly on the newest data, automatically, with no review. Judge that policy.

options.text: Sound — fresher data always means a better model
options.misconception: Assumes new data is always good data, with nothing to catch a bad night.

options.text: Unsound — models should be trained once and left alone
options.misconception: Over-corrects into a policy that guarantees drift goes unaddressed.

options.text: Reasonable only with a gate: each candidate must beat the current model on a held-out set before replacing it
Unsound, because nightly training is too expensive to justify
options.misconception: Raises cost, which is a real factor but not the governing risk of unreviewed automatic replacement.

hints: Ask what happens the night the incoming data is corrupted or unrepresentative.
The question is not whether to retrain but what must be true before the new model is allowed to serve.
explanation_after: Frequent retraining counters drift, but automatic promotion lets one bad day reach production. An evaluation gate plus the ability to roll back is what makes the automation safe — the same shape as the deployment gate for any risky change.

stem: A team has a million unlabelled support tickets and budget to label 2,000. They want automatic routing to one of eight teams. What is the best use of that budget?

options.text: Skip labelling and cluster all million tickets, using the clusters as the routing categories
options.misconception: Uses all the data but discovers its own groups, which need not line up with the eight teams the tickets must actually reach.

options.text: Label 2,000 tickets with the eight real team names and train a supervised classifier
Label 2,000 at random with no scheme, to keep the sample unbiased
options.misconception: Keeps the sampling honest but produces labels that do not name the eight destinations, so nothing can be routed.

options.text: Spend the budget on a larger model instead of labels
options.misconception: Capacity cannot substitute for a target; without labels there is nothing to learn to predict.

hints: The destination categories already exist and are fixed. Ask whether discovery is what is needed.
Ask what clusters would be named, and whether those names would match the eight teams.
explanation_after: The eight teams are given, so this is classification, not discovery. Clusters might split by topic in ways that cross team boundaries, leaving a mapping problem. 2,000 labels across eight classes is a workable start — and clustering is still useful for choosing which 2,000 to label.

stem: You are planning the development cycle for a spam-detection model. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Collect and label data → train → evaluate on held-out data → deploy → monitor for drift
Deploy → collect data → train → evaluate
options.misconception: Ships before there is a model, inverting the order entirely.

options.text: Train → collect data → deploy → label data
options.misconception: Trains before data exists and labels after deployment, when the labels were needed first.

options.text: Monitor for drift → deploy → train → collect data
options.misconception: Reverses the pipeline; monitoring is what follows a deployment, not what precedes a model.

hints: Ask which step produces something the next step needs.
The cycle ends with something that sends you back to the beginning.
explanation_after: Each stage feeds the next, and monitoring closes the loop by revealing when retraining is due. The cycle is iterative, not a line — which is why drift detection points back at data collection.

stem: Building a spam classifier from raw email text and a send timestamp, which engineered feature is genuinely useful?

options.text: The exact millisecond of the timestamp, since precision helps
options.misconception: Adds resolution with no relationship to spamminess, giving the model noise to overfit.

options.text: The number of exclamation marks in the text, since spam often over-punctuates
The email's size rounded to the nearest gigabyte
options.misconception: Rounds away all variation, so the column is constant and carries no information.

options.text: A random number attached to each email
options.misconception: Pure noise, which can only encourage spurious fitting.

hints: A good feature has to vary across examples and relate to the thing being predicted.
Check each candidate against both tests — some vary but mean nothing, one does not vary at all.
explanation_after: Exclamation count varies and plausibly relates to spam. Millisecond precision varies but means nothing; gigabyte rounding means something but no longer varies. Useful features need both.

stem: You are building a training set to tell cats from dogs in photos. Which labelling approach sets up supervised learning correctly?

options.text: Attach a cat-or-dog label to every photo, giving a ground truth to learn from and be checked against
Collect photos with no labels and let the model infer them
options.misconception: Describes unsupervised learning, which cannot produce the named categories the task requires.

options.text: Label only the cat photos and leave the dog photos unlabelled
options.misconception: Leaves the model unable to tell a dog from an unlabelled cat, since absence of a label means nothing.

options.text: Use each photo's file size as its label
options.misconception: Supplies a target unrelated to the question being asked.

hints: Supervised learning needs a known answer for every example it learns from.
Ask what the model would conclude from a photo carrying no label at all.
explanation_after: Every training photo needs its true class, so the model can measure error and be scored honestly later. Partial labelling leaves ambiguity the model cannot resolve.

stem: You have two years of daily sales and want to predict next month's. How should the data be split for evaluation?

options.text: Shuffle all days and take a random 20% as the test set
options.misconception: Lets the model train on days after those it is tested on, so it predicts the past from the future.

options.text: Train on the earliest 18 months and test on the most recent 6, preserving time order
Train and test on all the data, then compare against the training score
options.misconception: Leaves no unseen data at all, so the score measures memorisation.

options.text: Split by day of the week, training on weekdays and testing on weekends
options.misconception: Creates a systematic difference between the splits, so the test measures weekday-to-weekend transfer rather than forecasting.

hints: Ask what information the model will genuinely have when it makes a real prediction.
Make the evaluation imitate the real situation as closely as you can.
explanation_after: Forecasting means predicting forward, so the split must respect time. A shuffled split leaks future information — the model learns from Wednesday to predict Tuesday, and scores far better offline than it ever will in use.

stem: Your model shows clear overfitting: training accuracy 98%, validation 61%. Which plan is the soundest first response?

options.text: Train for more epochs so validation accuracy catches up
options.misconception: Continues the process that caused the gap; the validation score will usually fall further.

options.text: Report the 98% figure, since it is the model's best measured performance
options.misconception: Reports the number that is known not to generalise, which is the one measurement that cannot be trusted.

options.text: Add more training data if possible, and otherwise simplify the model or add regularisation and early stopping
Switch to a larger model with more parameters
options.misconception: Adds capacity to a model that is already memorising, which typically widens the gap.

hints: The model has more capacity than the data supports. Ask which side of that you can change.
Two directions are available: more evidence, or less freedom to memorise.
explanation_after: Overfitting is capacity exceeding evidence, so either raise the evidence or lower the capacity. More data is usually best; where it is unavailable, regularisation, a smaller model and early stopping all cut the freedom to memorise.

stem: A clinic wants AI help with diagnosis. Which scope is both useful and defensible given what current models can do?

options.text: The model issues the final diagnosis, and clinicians review only disputed cases
options.misconception: Makes the model the decision-maker and relies on someone disputing a result they may never see.

options.text: The model diagnoses routine cases and refers only unusual ones to a clinician
options.misconception: Sounds moderate but still makes the model the decider for the majority, and 'routine' is exactly what it may misjudge.

options.text: The model is used only for research and never informs any clinical work
options.misconception: Safe but forfeits the benefit entirely; the question asks for something useful as well as defensible.

options.text: The model flags findings for a clinician to confirm, and its confidence and reasoning are shown

hints: Ask who holds the decision and the accountability in each design.
A useful scope changes what the clinician sees without replacing their judgment.
explanation_after: Assisting keeps a qualified human accountable while still surfacing findings they might miss, and showing confidence lets them weigh it. The designs that hand over routine cases sound cautious but move the decision anyway.
